summary: A straight-line model can draw curves if you hand it x², x³ and so on.
headline: Curves from a line-fitting machine
overview: Add the square and the cube of x as extra columns. The model is still linear in its weights, but the curve it draws can bend.
Higher degrees bend more. Play through them and watch what changes.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Slide the degree to 9 on only 14 points. The curve starts chasing individual dots.

check.question: Why is polynomial regression still called linear regression?
options: The curve is a straight line
It is linear in the weights
It only works on two points

realLife: Spline and basis-function models in analytics tools are this same idea with smarter columns.
data: Fourteen training points from a sine wave plus noise. The dashed line is the true pattern, which a real project would not know.
maths: ŷ = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x² + … + w_d x^d
Build columns x, x², …, x^d, then run ordinary least squares.
Here x is mapped to [−1, 1] first, because raw powers are badly scaled.
code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(5), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())
